discoveryHook.scenario: Think of absolute value as a measure of distance from zero. If you're 5 steps away from home, you could be 5 steps east or 5 steps west. Absolute value equations capture that 'either‑or' idea — and solving them unlocks two possible positions!

explanation: An [[kw:absolute value equation]] contains an absolute value expression, like $ |x| = a $.
Because absolute value is always non‑negative, $ |ax + b| = c $ has [[imp:no solution if $ c < 0 $]].
When $ c \ge 0 $, rewrite the equation as two [[imp:related linear equations]]: $ ax + b = c $ or $ ax + b = -c $.
Solve each linear equation separately. Both are possible solutions.
Always check your answers in the original equation.

rows.1: $ ax + b = c $ or $ ax + b = -c $

formulaCard.title: Absolute Value Equation
notes: Absolute value is distance from zero, never negative.
formulaCard.formula: $$ |ax + b| = c \quad\Rightarrow\quad ax + b = c \;\text{or}\; ax + b = -c $$

examples.title: A – Two Positive Solutions
steps: Since $ 6 \ge 0 $, write two equations: $ x - 4 = 6 $ or $ x - 4 = -6 $.
Graph: points at -2 and 10, both 6 units away from 4.
examples.prompt: Solve $ |x - 4| = 6 $. Graph the solutions on a number line.

steps: The absolute value of any expression is always $ \ge 0 $.
It can never equal a negative number like -5.
So the equation has no solution.
examples.title: B – No Solution Case
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why does this equation have no solution, without doing any algebra?

steps: Write two equations: $ w = 6 $ or $ w = -6 $.
examples.title: C – A Simple Case

hints: Absolute value gives two opposite numbers.
questions.prompt: The equation $ |x| = 5 $ is equivalent to $ x = 5 $ or $ x = $ ___.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: Absolute value cannot equal -2, so there are no solutions.

questions.prompt: What must be true about $ c $ for $ |ax + b| = c $ to have solutions?
hints: Think about the definition of absolute value.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: c must be greater than or equal to 0.

teacherCues: Write |x+2|=3 on the board. Ask: 'What numbers can x+2 be to have an absolute value of 3?'
Draw a number line showing a point and its opposite, each the same distance from zero.

confusionCorner.body: If you see $ |something| = \text{negative} $, there is [[imp:no solution]]. Don't waste time writing two equations — the absolute value can't be negative.
confusionCorner.title: Negative Right‑Hand Side? Stop!

blocks.title: Solving Absolute Value Equations

questions.prompt: What is the first step in solving $ |m + 3| - 7 = 0 $?
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Add 7 to both sides to isolate the absolute value.

questions.prompt: Solve $ 3|p| = 12 $. What is one possible value of $ p $?
Before splitting an absolute value equation into two cases, make sure the absolute value is ___ on one side.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The absolute value must be isolated (alone) on one side.
hints: No other numbers attached to it.

blocks.title: Isolating the Absolute Value First
teacherCues: Write $ |3x + 9| - 10 = -4 $ on the board. Ask: 'What is different about this equation compared to the last one?'
Demonstrate adding 10 to both sides to isolate the absolute value before splitting.

examples.title: A – Add First, Then Split
steps: Write two equations: $ x - 2 = 4 $ or $ x - 2 = -4 $.

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why must we divide by 4 before writing the two equations?
examples.title: B – Multiplying to Isolate

confusionCorner.body: If you write two equations before isolating, you'll get incorrect results. In $ |x - 2| + 5 = 9 $, do not write $ x - 2 + 5 = 9 $ and $ x - 2 + 5 = -9 $. The absolute value bars act as a container — the +5 is outside.
confusionCorner.title: Don't Split Too Early

rows.1: Undo addition/subtraction outside the absolute value.

notes: Treat the absolute value bars like parentheses — undo outside operations first.
formulaCard.title: Isolate First

explanation: If the absolute value expression is combined with other terms, [[imp:isolate it on one side]] first.
Use inverse operations (add, subtract, multiply, divide) to get $ |expression| = \text{number} $.
Then apply the standard method: split into two equations.
Never split until the absolute value is completely alone.

discoveryHook.scenario: Sometimes the absolute value is trapped with other numbers. Like digging for treasure, you need to isolate it — get it alone on one side — before you can unlock its two hidden solutions.

confusionCorner.title: Midpoint vs. Average
confusionCorner.body: The midpoint is just the average of the min and max. But the distance is half the range. Don't accidentally use the full range as the distance — it's the distance from the center to one side.

discoveryHook.scenario: A soccer ball must weigh between 410 g and 450 g. Instead of writing two inequalities, you can capture the whole range with one sleek absolute value equation. That's the power of absolute value as a distance from the center!

questions.prompt: If a range is 10 to 20, what is the midpoint?
hints: Add the min and max, then divide by 2.

questions.prompt: If the midpoint is 50 and the distance is 5, what is the absolute value equation? (Use x as the variable.)
To write an absolute value equation from a range, you need to find the ___ (average of min and max) and the distance to each endpoint.
hints: It's the center point of the interval.

blocks.title: Writing Absolute Value Equations
teacherCues: Display a number line with min 4 and max 5. Ask: 'What is the midpoint? The distance from the midpoint to each endpoint?'
Guide: midpoint = (min+max)/2, distance = (max-min)/2. Equation: |x - midpoint| = distance.

visuals.title: From Range to Absolute Value Equation

explanation: If you know the minimum and maximum acceptable values, you can write an absolute value equation.
Find the [[imp:midpoint]]: $ \frac{\text{min} + \text{max}}{2} $.
Find the [[imp:distance]] from the midpoint to either endpoint: $ \frac{\text{max} - \text{min}}{2} $.
The equation is $ |x - \text{midpoint}| = \text{distance} $.
To solve $ |ax + b| = |cx + d| $, write two equations: $ ax + b = cx + d $ or $ ax + b = -(cx + d) $.
Solve both. Each may give a solution.
An [[kw:extraneous solution]] is a value that arises from solving but does [[imp:not satisfy the original equation]].
Always check your solutions in the original equation, especially when absolute values appear on both sides.

notes: Check every solution; extraneous ones are possible.
If one equation gives a false statement, ignore it.
formulaCard.title: Two Absolute Values
formulaCard.formula: $$ |ax + b| = |cx + d| \;\Rightarrow\; ax + b = cx + d \;\text{or}\; ax + b = -(cx + d) $$

discoveryHook.scenario: When two absolute values face off, like $ |3x - 4| = |x| $, the expressions inside could be equal, or they could be opposites. And sometimes, a solution that pops out of your algebra doesn't actually fit the original equation — an imposter! That's an extraneous solution, and you must check to expose it.

blocks.title: Two Absolute Values & Extraneous Solutions

examples.title: A – Two Absolute Values
steps: Solve first: $ 2x = 4 \Rightarrow x = 2 $. Solve second: $ 4x = 4 \Rightarrow x = 1 $.

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why is $ x = -2 $ extraneous? What goes wrong when you plug it in?
examples.title: B – Extraneous Solution
steps: Check $ x=6 $: $ |24| = 24 $ ✓. Check $ x=-2 $: $ |8| = -8 $? No — absolute value cannot equal a negative.
$ x = -2 $ is extraneous. Only $ x = 6 $ is a solution.
examples.prompt: Solve $ |2x + 12| = 4x $ and check for extraneous solutions.

questions.prompt: A solution that appears from algebra but does not satisfy the original equation is called an ___ solution.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: The equations give x=7 and x=-3; the smaller is -3.
questions.prompt: Solve $ |x + 8| = |2x + 1| $. What is the smaller of the two solutions?
hints: Set up the two equations: x+8 = 2x+1 and x+8 = -(2x+1).
Solve both equations, then choose the smaller number.

questions.answer: absolute value cannot equal a negative
hints: Can absolute value equal a negative number?
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Because the right side becomes -8, and absolute value can't be negative.

teacherCues: Write $ |3x - 4| = |x| $ on the board. Ask: 'If two absolute values are equal, what can we say about the expressions inside?'
Introduce the term 'extraneous solution' with the example $ |2x + 12| = 4x $.

confusionCorner.title: Always Check!
confusionCorner.body: Extraneous solutions often appear when the absolute value is set equal to a variable expression (like $ 4x $) that could be negative. The absolute value on the left is non‑negative, so the right side must be non‑negative. If a solution makes the right side negative, reject it.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Absolute Value Problems
teacherCues: Display the Understand → Solve → Conclude framework. Walk through a real‑world absolute value problem, labeling each phase.
Emphasize that 'Understand' includes recognizing the absolute value structure and isolating if needed.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: First isolate the absolute value: subtract 2 from both sides.
hints: It's not yet in the form $ |...| = c $.
questions.prompt: In the blueprint, what is the first step when you see an equation like $ |x - 3| + 2 = 7 $?
After splitting into two equations, you must ___ each candidate solution in the original equation to check for extraneous results.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: You must check each solution to see if it works.

questions.prompt: If the range of acceptable values is 10 to 20, what is the absolute value equation? (Use $ x $ as the variable, write as |x - a| = b with numbers.)

confusionCorner.title: Interpreting the Two Solutions
confusionCorner.body: In a distance problem like the car example, two solutions make sense: one when the car is approaching, and one after it passes. Don't discard a solution just because it's larger — it may be physically meaningful.

explanation: The [[imp:Understand → Solve → Conclude]] blueprint helps you break down any absolute value problem.
[[imp:Understand]]: Identify whether you're solving an equation or writing one from a range. Isolate the absolute value if needed.
[[imp:Solve]]: Split into two linear equations, solve both, and check for extraneous solutions.
[[imp:Conclude]]: State the solution(s) clearly, with units if applicable, and verify against the original context.

formulaCard.title: Blueprint in One Line
notes: Only after isolating the absolute value.
Check each candidate in the original equation.

rows.1: Identify the equation or range; isolate absolute value.
Split into two cases; solve each; check for extraneous solutions.
State solutions; interpret in context if real‑world problem.

examples.title: A – Car Distance Problem
steps: Understand: Set $ |300 - 48t| = 60 $. This is an absolute value equation.
Conclude: The car is 60 ft away at 5 seconds (approaching) and again at 7.5 seconds (after passing).
examples.prompt: A car starts 300 ft away and drives toward you at 48 ft/s. Its distance from you after $ t $ seconds is $ d = |300 - 48t| $. When is the car 60 ft away?

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: How do you know the equation is $ |x - 68| = 5 $?
steps: Conclude: The true percentage is between 63% and 73%.
examples.prompt: A survey says 68% favor year‑round school, with a ±5% error. Write and solve an absolute value equation to find the actual minimum and maximum percentages.
examples.title: B – Survey Tolerance

examples.prompt: A part must be 50 mm long with a tolerance of ±0.2 mm. Write the absolute value equation and find the minimum and maximum acceptable lengths.
steps: Conclude: Acceptable lengths are between 49.8 mm and 50.2 mm.
examples.title: C – Tolerances in Manufacturing

discoveryHook.scenario: From tolerance in manufacturing to distances on a number line, absolute value problems follow a clear blueprint. Understand the situation, solve the equation, and conclude with the real‑world meaning. No more guesswork!

title: Chapter 1.4 — Solving Absolute Value Equations
presenterNotes: The key to absolute value equations is the 'two cases' idea. Use a number line to show distance = absolute value.
When isolating, physically circle the absolute value bars and say 'this must be alone'.
Extraneous solutions are a new concept; spend extra time on checking solutions. The car distance example naturally shows why both times are valid.
